### Subject: Opinion on deductibility of interest on Compulsorily Convertible Debentures and applicability of thin-capitalisation rules

---

## 1. Purpose and Basis of this Opinion

This opinion is issued pursuant to our engagement letter dated [●], and is based solely on the facts and representations furnished by the management of Hillcrest Realty Private Limited, and on the relevant provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961, applicable rules, notifications, circulars, and judicial precedents as they stand on the date hereof. ## 2. Statement of Facts

Hillcrest Realty Private Limited issued Compulsorily Convertible Debentures of INR 100 crore to its Singapore parent, Hillcrest Global Pte Ltd, carrying an 11% annual coupon and mandatorily convertible into equity after 10 years. Annual interest expense is INR 11 crore, against EBITDA of INR 60 crore.

## 3. Issue for Consideration

Whether the coupon on the CCDs is deductible as interest under Section 36(1)(iii), and whether the thin-capitalisation restriction under Section 94B limits the deduction.

## 4. Relevant Legal Framework

- Section 36(1)(iii)
- Section 2(28A)
- Section 94B


## 5. Judicial Precedents Considered

- CIT v. Rajshree Sugars & Chemicals Ltd (Mad HC)

## 6. Analysis

For income-tax purposes, CCDs are treated as debt until the date of actual conversion, notwithstanding their compound-instrument classification under Ind AS 32, so the coupon qualifies as deductible 'interest'. As the interest is paid to a non-resident associated enterprise and exceeds INR 1 crore, Section 94B caps the deduction at the lower of the actual interest paid (INR 11 crore) or 30% of EBITDA (INR 18 crore); since actual interest is well within the 30% EBITDA ceiling, no disallowance arises.

## 7. Conclusion / Opinion

The full interest of INR 11 crore is deductible under Section 36(1)(iii); Section 94B does not result in any disallowance on the present facts.

**Confidence level:** High
